reminder: A reducible configuration is a small subgraph that a minimal counterexample to the four colour theorem cannot contain.
definition: In the study of the four colour theorem, a configuration is a connected piece of a triangulated [planar graph](c:planar-graph) with given vertex [degrees](c:vertex-degree), surrounded by a ring of vertices. It is reducible when every proper 4-[colouring](c:graph-coloring) of the graph outside it can be changed, for example by swapping colours along [Kempe chains](c:kempe-chain), into a colouring that extends over the configuration. Then a minimal counterexample, a smallest planar [graph](c:graph) that needs five colours, cannot contain it.
examples: A vertex of degree 4 in a triangulation is reducible: Kempe's chain argument recolours its neighbours so that one colour stays free for the vertex.
The Birkhoff diamond, four vertices of degree 5 that form a diamond inside a ring of 6 vertices, is reducible.
Non-example: A single vertex of degree 5 is not reducible by the Kempe chain argument, and this is the gap that Heawood found in Kempe's proof.

reminder: A refinement of a family is a second family in which every member maps into some member of the first.
definition: Let $U=(U_i)_{i\in I}$ and $V=(V_j)_{j\in J}$ be families of objects of a [category](c:category). The family $V$ refines $U$ when there is a [function](c:function) $f:J\to I$ of indices and a morphism $V_j\to U_{f(j)}$ for every $j\in J$. For [open covers](c:open-cover) of a space, this says that every set of $V$ lies inside some set of $U$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$, the cover by the intervals $(k-1,k+1)$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ refines the cover $\{(-\infty,2),(-1,\infty)\}$, because each interval lies in one of the two sets.
A subcover of an [open cover](c:open-cover) refines it, with $f$ the inclusion of the index sets.
Non-example: The cover $\{(-\infty,2),(-1,\infty)\}$ does not refine the cover by the intervals $(k-1,k+1)$, because the set $(-1,\infty)$ lies in no single interval.

reminder: A reflection group is a group of linear maps of a vector space that is generated by reflections.
definition: A reflection group is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $W$ of the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $GL(V)$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ that is generated by reflections. A reflection is a non-identity element of finite order that fixes a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) pointwise; over $\mathbb{R}$ with an inner product, the orthogonal ones are the [reflections in a hyperplane](c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane).
examples: The symmetric group $S_n$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by permuting coordinates, and the transpositions are the reflections in the hyperplanes $x_i=x_j$.
The dihedral group of order $2m$ acts on the plane and is generated by two reflections in lines at the angle $\pi/m$.
Non-example: The group of three rotations of the real plane, by $0$, $2\pi/3$ and $4\pi/3$, contains no reflection, so it is not a reflection group.

steps: Let $G=GL(V)$ be the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) of $V$ and let $T$ be a set of reflections in $G$.
The set of all finite products of elements of $T$ and their inverses contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses.
So it is a subgroup of $G$, and the added condition is that reflections generate it.
links.why: It shows that a reflection group is a subgroup chosen by its generators, so its elements are words in reflections.

steps: Take a Coxeter group $W$ with generators $S$ and [Coxeter matrix](c:coxeter-matrix) $m$.
Let $V$ be the real vector space with basis $S$ and let $B$ be the symmetric bilinear form defined by $m$.
Each generator $s$ acts on $V$ as a reflection that fixes a hyperplane pointwise.
This action of $W$ on $V$ is faithful, so $W$ is a reflection group.
links.why: It shows that every Coxeter group is a reflection group, so results about reflection groups apply to Coxeter groups.

reminder: A Banach space is reflexive when every element of its double dual comes from an element of the space.
definition: A [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ is reflexive if the canonical map $J:X\to X^{**}$, given by $J(x)(\varphi)=\varphi(x)$, is surjective. Here $X^{**}$ is the [bidual](c:bidual), the [dual space](c:dual-space) of the dual of $X$. The map $J$ is always an isometric embedding, so $J$ is then an isometric isomorphism.
examples: Every finite-dimensional normed space is reflexive, because $J$ is injective and $X$ and $X^{**}$ have the same finite dimension.
The [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^p[0,1]$ with $1<p<\infty$ is reflexive: its dual is $L^q$ with $1/p+1/q=1$, and the dual of $L^q$ is $L^p$.
Non-example: The space $\ell^1$ is not reflexive, because a Banach limit on $\ell^\infty$ is an element of $(\ell^\infty)^*=(\ell^1)^{**}$ that no element of $\ell^1$ gives.

steps: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
The Riesz representation theorem identifies $H$ with its [dual space](c:dual-space) by an isometric conjugate-linear bijection.
Apply this identification twice to see that every functional on $H^*$ is evaluation at a point of $H$.
So the canonical map $H\to H^{**}$ is onto, and $H$ is reflexive.
links.why: It shows that every Hilbert space is reflexive, so reflexive spaces include all Hilbert spaces and all the $L^p$ spaces with $1<p<\infty$.

steps: Take a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ with its canonical map $J:X\to X^{**}$.
The map $J$ is always a linear isometry, so it is injective and has closed range.
The added condition for reflexivity is that $J$ is also surjective.
links.why: It shows that reflexivity is one extra condition on a Banach space: the canonical map into the bidual is onto.

reminder: A regular category has finite limits, coequalizers of kernel pairs, and regular epimorphisms that are stable under pullback.
definition: A category $C$ is regular if it has all [finite limits](c:finite-limit), if every [kernel pair](c:kernel-pair) has a [coequalizer](c:coequalizer), and if the [pullback](c:pullback) of a [regular epimorphism](c:is-regular-epi) along any morphism is again a regular epimorphism. In such a category every morphism factors as a regular epimorphism followed by a monomorphism, and this factorization is stable under pullback.
examples: The category of sets is regular: regular epimorphisms are surjections, and the pullback of a surjection is a surjection.
Every [abelian category](c:abelian-category) and every [topos](c:topos) is regular, and so is the category of groups.
Non-example: The category of topological spaces is not regular, because its regular epimorphisms are the quotient maps, and a pullback of a quotient map need not be a quotient map.

steps: Take a regular category $C$.
By definition $C$ has all finite limits, so it is a [finitely complete category](c:finitely-complete-category).
The added conditions are coequalizers of kernel pairs and the pullback stability of regular epimorphisms.
links.why: It shows what a regular category adds to finite limits: a good theory of images and quotients.

steps: Take a [coherent category](c:coherent-category) $C$.
By definition $C$ is a regular category in which every poset of subobjects has finite unions that pullback preserves.
Forget the finite unions, and what remains is a regular category.
links.why: It shows that every coherent category is regular, so facts about regular categories apply to all coherent categories.

steps: Take an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) $A$, which has all finite limits.
In $A$ every epimorphism is the cokernel of its kernel, and the kernel pair of a morphism $f$ has the coequalizer $\operatorname{im}f$.
Epimorphisms in $A$ are stable under pullback, so $A$ is a regular category.
links.why: It shows that regular categories include all abelian categories, so exactness arguments for abelian categories use only regularity.

reminder: A regular graph is a graph in which every vertex has the same degree.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) is $k$-regular if every [vertex](c:vertex) has [degree](c:vertex-degree) exactly $k$. A graph is regular when it is $k$-regular for some $k$.
examples: The cycle on $n\ge3$ vertices is 2-regular, and the Petersen graph is 3-regular.
The [complete graph](c:complete-graph) on $n$ vertices is $(n-1)$-regular.
Non-example: The path with three vertices is not regular, because its two ends have degree 1 and its middle vertex has degree 2.

steps: Take a [graph](c:graph) $G$ and compute the [degree](c:vertex-degree) of each vertex.
The added condition is that all these degrees take one common value $k$.
links.why: It shows that regularity is a condition on the degree function of a graph, so counting arguments with edges and degrees apply.

steps: Take a [complete graph](c:complete-graph) on $n$ vertices.
Each vertex is joined to the other $n-1$ vertices and to nothing else.
So every vertex has degree $n-1$, and the graph is $(n-1)$-regular.
links.why: It shows that complete graphs are the densest regular graphs, so they are the first examples to test a claim about regular graphs.

reminder: A regular polyhedron has congruent regular polygons as faces and the same number of faces at every vertex.
definition: A regular convex [polyhedron](c:polyhedron) is a polyhedron whose faces are all congruent regular polygons and in which the same number of faces meet at every [vertex](c:vertex). There are exactly five such polyhedra: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.
examples: The [cube](c:cube) has six congruent squares as faces, with three squares at each vertex.
The [icosahedron](c:icosahedron) has twenty equilateral triangles as faces, with five triangles at each vertex.
Non-example: The triangular bipyramid has six equilateral triangles as faces, but three faces meet at some vertices and four at others, so it is not regular.

steps: Take a convex [polyhedron](c:polyhedron) $P$.
Require that all faces of $P$ are congruent regular polygons.
Require that the same number of faces meet at every vertex of $P$.
links.why: It shows that regularity adds two uniformity conditions, one on the faces and one on the vertices.

steps: A [regular polytope](c:regular-polytope) is a polytope whose symmetry group acts transitively on its flags, the chains of a vertex, an edge and a face.
The symmetry group of a regular convex polyhedron such as the cube acts transitively on its flags.
So a regular polyhedron is a regular polytope of dimension 3.
links.why: It shows that the five regular polyhedra are the three-dimensional case of regular polytopes, which exist in every dimension.

reminder: A singular point of a linear differential equation is regular when its coefficients have poles of low enough order.
definition: Consider the [linear differential equation](c:linear-differential-equation) $y^{(n)}+p_1(z)y^{(n-1)}+\dots+p_n(z)y=0$ with [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) coefficients $p_k$. A point $z_0$ where some $p_k$ has a [pole](c:pole) is a regular singular point when every $p_k$ has a pole of order at most $k$ at $z_0$. Equivalently, each $(z-z_0)^kp_k$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) at $z_0$.
examples: The Bessel equation $z^2y''+zy'+(z^2-\nu^2)y=0$ has a regular singular point at $z=0$, since $p_1=1/z$ and $p_2=1-\nu^2/z^2$ have poles of order 1 and 2.
The Euler equation $z^2y''+\alpha zy'+\beta y=0$ has a regular singular point at $0$, and its solutions are powers $z^r$.
Non-example: The equation $z^2y'+y=0$ has an irregular singular point at $0$, because $p_1=1/z^2$ has a pole of order 2, and the solution $e^{1/z}$ has an essential singularity.

reminder: Relative homology of a space and a subspace is the homology of the chains of the space taken modulo the chains of the subspace.
definition: Let $A\subseteq X$ be a subspace of a [topological space](c:topological-space). The relative chain complex is the [quotient chain complex](c:quotient-chain-complex) $C_\bullet(X,A)=C_\bullet(X)/C_\bullet(A)$ of singular [chain complexes](c:chain-complex), and its cycles are the chains of $X$ whose boundary lies in $A$. The relative homology $H_n(X,A)$ is the [homology](c:homology) of $C_\bullet(X,A)$ in degree $n$.
examples: For $A=\emptyset$ the relative homology $H_n(X,\emptyset)$ is the ordinary homology $H_n(X)$.
For the disc and its boundary sphere with $n\ge1$, $H_k(D^n,S^{n-1})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ if $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
Non-example: Neither $H_n(X)$ nor $H_n(A)$ nor their sum is $H_n(X,A)$; the three groups only fit into a long exact sequence.

steps: Take any [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and the empty subspace $A=\emptyset$.
The chain complex $C_\bullet(\emptyset)$ is zero, so $C_\bullet(X)/C_\bullet(\emptyset)=C_\bullet(X)$.
Hence $H_n(X,\emptyset)=H_n(X)$, and ordinary homology is the case $A=\emptyset$.
links.why: It shows that every statement about relative homology contains the case of ordinary homology.

reminder: The relative homotopy group $\pi_n(X,A)$ classifies maps of the $n$-disc into $X$ whose boundary sphere lands in $A$.
definition: Let $A\subseteq X$ be a subspace of a [pointed space](c:pointed-space) with base point $x_0\in A$. For $n\ge1$, $\pi_n(X,A,x_0)$ is the set of [homotopy](c:homotopy) classes of maps $(D^n,S^{n-1},s_0)\to(X,A,x_0)$, where homotopies keep the boundary sphere in $A$ and the base point fixed. It is a group for $n\ge2$, like a [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group), and it is abelian for $n\ge3$.
examples: For $A=\{x_0\}$ the group $\pi_n(X,\{x_0\},x_0)$ is the ordinary homotopy group $\pi_n(X,x_0)$, because the boundary sphere goes to a point.
For $n\ge2$, $\pi_n(D^n,S^{n-1},s_0)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the identity map of the pair.
Non-example: Free homotopy classes of maps $D^n\to X$, with no condition on the boundary, only count the path components of $X$, so they are not a relative homotopy group.

steps: Take a [pointed space](c:pointed-space) $(X,x_0)$ and the subspace $A=\{x_0\}$.
A map $(D^n,S^{n-1},s_0)\to(X,\{x_0\},x_0)$ sends the boundary sphere to the base point.
Such a map is the same as a based map $S^n=D^n/S^{n-1}\to X$, so $\pi_n(X,\{x_0\},x_0)=\pi_n(X,x_0)$.
links.why: It shows that ordinary homotopy groups are the relative groups for the smallest choice of subspace.

reminder: Renormalization is the choice of an extension of time-ordered products to coinciding spacetime points, where the naive products are undefined.
definition: In perturbative quantum field theory, the [time-ordered products](c:time-ordered-product) of the interaction are defined as [distributions](c:distribution) away from coinciding points but are ill defined on the diagonal. Renormalization is the choice of an [extension of these distributions](c:extension-of-distributions) to the diagonal that keeps the required properties, such as causality, and the choice is unique only up to local terms. These choices fix the [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) of a given [Lagrangian density](c:lagrangian-density) order by order.
examples: In $\phi^4$ theory in four spacetime dimensions, the square $\Delta_F(x-y)^2$ of the Feynman propagator is defined for $x\ne y$, and its extensions to $x=y$ differ by a multiple $c\,\delta(x-y)$ of the delta distribution.
Non-example: A momentum cutoff alone is a regularization, because it makes each integral finite but does not fix the finite parts that the limit leaves free.
Non-example: A free theory with a quadratic Lagrangian has no interaction vertices, so no ill-defined products of propagators arise and no renormalization is needed.

steps: The time-ordered products are [distributions](c:distribution) on the complement of the diagonal in the space of point configurations.
Defining them on the whole space is an instance of the extension problem for distributions.
Renormalization adds the conditions of causality, covariance and bounded scaling degree to this problem.
links.why: It shows that renormalization is a precise extension problem, and that its ambiguity is the space of local terms of bounded scaling degree.

reminder: The renormalization group consists of the changes between choices of renormalization, and it also describes how a theory changes under scaling.
definition: In perturbative quantum field theory, two choices of [renormalization](c:renormalization) for the same [Lagrangian density](c:lagrangian-density) differ by a finite redefinition of the interaction vertices. These redefinitions form a [group](c:group) that acts on the space of interactions, and a change of the energy scale or cutoff moves a [renormalization scheme](c:renormalization-scheme) along a [renormalization group flow](c:renormalization-group-flow).
examples: In $\phi^4$ theory, the coupling $\lambda$ changes with the energy scale $\mu$ by $\mu\,d\lambda/d\mu=\beta(\lambda)$, with $\beta(\lambda)=3\lambda^2/(16\pi^2)$ at one loop.
In quantum electrodynamics, the renormalization group flow makes the effective charge grow with the energy scale.
Non-example: The Poincaré group is a symmetry group of the theory, and it does not relate different choices of renormalization.

reminder: A repeated game is a game in which the players play the same stage game again and again and see the earlier play.
definition: A repeated game is an [extensive-form game](c:extensive-form-game) built from a fixed one-shot stage game, which the players play in rounds $t=1,2,\dots$, finitely or infinitely often. In each round a player chooses an action after seeing the history of earlier rounds, and the payoff is a sum, an average or a discounted sum of the stage payoffs.
examples: The prisoner's dilemma played 100 times in a row, with total payoff the sum of the 100 stage payoffs.
A Cournot duopoly in which two firms choose quantities every year for ever, with payoff the discounted sum of yearly profits.
Non-example: A one-shot game is not a repeated game, because it has one round and so no history on which a player can condition an action.

steps: A repeated game has a game tree in which each node is the history of the rounds played so far.
At each node every player chooses an action of the stage game, so each round is one layer of the tree.
The payoff of a play is a sum or discounted sum of the stage payoffs, so the tree repeats the same structure.
links.why: It shows that repeated games inherit the notions of strategy and equilibrium of extensive-form games.

reminder: The representation category of a group has its representations as objects and equivariant linear maps as morphisms.
definition: For a [group](c:group) $G$ and a field $k$, the representation category $\mathrm{Rep}(G)$ has as objects the [group representations](c:group-representation) of $G$ on $k$-vector spaces, often only finite-dimensional ones. Its morphisms are the [equivariant](c:equivariant-map) [linear maps](c:linear-map) between them, and the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) of representations makes it a monoidal category.
examples: For the trivial group, $\mathrm{Rep}(\{e\})$ is the category of $k$-vector spaces.
For a finite group $G$ and $k=\mathbb{C}$, every object of $\mathrm{Rep}(G)$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations.
For $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{C}$, there are exactly two irreducible representations, the trivial one and the sign.
Non-example: The set of irreducible representations of $G$ is not the representation category, because it has no direct sums, no tensor products and no morphisms.

steps: View the [group](c:group) $G$ as a category $BG$ with one object, whose morphisms are the elements of $G$.
A [functor](c:functor) $BG\to\mathrm{Vect}_k$ picks a vector space $V$ and a linear map $\rho(g)$ on $V$ for each $g$, compatible with products.
That data is a representation of $G$ on $V$.
A [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) between two such functors is one linear map that commutes with every $\rho(g)$, an equivariant map.
links.why: It shows that $\mathrm{Rep}(G)$ is the functor category $\mathrm{Fun}(BG,\mathrm{Vect}_k)$, so general facts on functor categories apply.

reminder: A representation of a C*-algebra is a *-homomorphism from the algebra into the bounded operators on a Hilbert space.
definition: A representation of a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a [star-algebra homomorphism](c:star-alg-hom) $\pi:A\to B(H)$ into the [bounded operators](c:bounded-operator) on $H$. That is, $\pi$ is linear and multiplicative, and $\pi(a^*)=\pi(a)^*$ for every $a\in A$.
examples: A concrete C*-algebra $A\subseteq B(H)$ is represented on $H$ by its inclusion map.
The algebra $C(X)$ of continuous functions on a compact space $X$ acts on $L^2(X,\mu)$ by multiplication, $\pi(f)g=fg$.
Every state of $A$ gives a representation on a Hilbert space built from the state, by the [GNS construction](c:gns-construction).
Non-example: On $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ the map $a\mapsto SaS^{-1}$ with $S=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ is linear and multiplicative, but $\pi(a^*)\ne\pi(a)^*$ for $a=E_{12}$, so it is not a representation.

steps: A [star-representation](c:star-representation) of a [star-algebra](c:star-algebra) is a homomorphism of star-algebras into linear operators on a dense subspace of a Hilbert space.
A C*-algebra is a star-algebra, and its representation $\pi:A\to B(H)$ is such a homomorphism.
The added condition is that all operators are bounded and defined on all of $H$.
links.why: It shows that C*-algebra representations are the bounded case of star-representations, where operator domains cause no trouble.

reminder: A representative function on a group is a matrix coefficient of a finite-dimensional representation of the group.
definition: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group), or an abstract group with the discrete topology, and $F$ a field. A function $f:G\to F$ is representative if $f(g)=t(\rho(g))$ for a continuous [representation](c:group-representation) $\rho:G\to\mathrm{End}(V)$ on a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) $V$ over $F$ and a [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $t$ on the space $\mathrm{End}(V)$ of [endomorphisms](c:endomorphism). Equivalently, the translates $x\mapsto f(gx)$ span a finite-dimensional space.
examples: A matrix entry $g\mapsto\rho(g)_{ij}$ of a finite-dimensional matrix representation is representative, and so is the character $g\mapsto\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$.
On the group $(\mathbb{R},+)$, the functions $e^{\lambda x}$, $\cos x$ and every polynomial are representative.
Non-example: On $(\mathbb{R},+)$ the function $e^{x^2}$ is not representative, because its translates $e^{x^2}e^{2ax}e^{a^2}$ span an infinite-dimensional space.

reminder: A residual is an object that turns maps out of a tensor product into maps into it, as a function set does.
definition: Let $(C,\otimes)$ be a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category). The left residual of objects $a,b$ is an object $a\backslash b$ with natural bijections $\mathrm{Hom}(a\otimes x,b)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(x,a\backslash b)$, and the right residual $b/a$ has $\mathrm{Hom}(x\otimes a,b)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(x,b/a)$. In a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) the two residuals agree.
examples: In the category of sets with the cartesian product, the residual of $a$ and $b$ is the [exponential object](c:exponential-object) $b^a$, the set of maps $a\to b$.
In a Heyting algebra, seen as a poset with $\otimes=\wedge$, the residual is the implication $a\Rightarrow b$.
In a quantale, the left residual $a\backslash b$ is the largest element $x$ with $a\cdot x\le b$.
Non-example: In the poset $(\mathbb{N},\le)$ with $\otimes=+$ the residual of $5$ and $3$ does not exist, because no $x$ satisfies $5+x\le3$.

steps: Take a [cartesian monoidal category](c:cartesian-monoidal-category), so that $\otimes$ is the categorical product.
This category is symmetric, so the left and right residuals of $a$ and $b$ agree.
The defining bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(a\times x,b)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(x,a\backslash b)$ is the one that defines an [exponential object](c:exponential-object) $b^a$.
So the residual is the exponential object when the tensor product is the product.
links.why: It shows that residuals extend exponential objects to monoidal categories that are not cartesian and not symmetric.

steps: A [residuated lattice](c:residuated-lattice) is a lattice with a monoid product $\cdot$ for which the residuals $a\backslash b$ and $b/a$ exist.
Regard it as a monoidal category: objects are the elements, morphisms are the order, and the tensor product is $\cdot$.
Then $a\cdot x\le b$ if and only if $x\le a\backslash b$ says that the residuals of the lattice are the residuals of this monoidal category.
links.why: It shows that the residuals of a residuated lattice are the order-theoretic case of residuals in a monoidal category.

reminder: The residue field of a local ring is its quotient by the unique maximal ideal.
definition: Let $R$ be a [local ring](c:local-ring) with unique [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$. Its residue field is the [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $R/\mathfrak m$, which is a [field](c:field) when $R$ is commutative. For a point $x$ of a scheme, the residue field $\kappa(x)$ is the residue field of the local ring of the scheme at $x$.
examples: For the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of fractions with denominator prime to $p$, the maximal ideal is $(p)$ and the residue field is $\mathbb{F}_p$.
For the local ring $k[x]_{(x)}$ the residue field is $k$, and the quotient map is evaluation at $0$.
Non-example: In the local ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ the quotient by $(p^2)$ is not a residue field, because $p$ is a nonzero nilpotent element there, so the quotient is not a field.

steps: Take a [local ring](c:local-ring) $R$ and an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of $R$ to form the [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $R/I$.
Choose $I$ to be the unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$.
The quotient by a maximal ideal of a commutative ring is a field, so $R/\mathfrak m$ is the residue field.
links.why: It shows that the residue field is the quotient that kills exactly the non-units of a local ring.

reminder: The Riemann curvature of a Riemannian manifold is the curvature of its Levi-Civita connection.
definition:
Let $(X,g)$ be a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection) $
abla$. Its Riemann curvature is the [curvature](c:curvature) of $
abla$, the tensor $R(U,V)W=
abla_U
abla_VW-
abla_V
abla_UW-
abla_{[U,V]}W$ for vector fields $U,V,W$.
examples: On Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ the Levi-Civita connection is the ordinary derivative, so $R=0$.
On the unit sphere $S^n$, $R(U,V)W=g(V,W)U-g(U,W)V$, so the sphere has constant sectional curvature 1.
Non-example: The [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) and the [scalar curvature](c:scalar-curvature) are traces of $R$, not $R$ itself, and they lose information in dimension 4 and higher.

steps: The curvature of a connection $\nabla$ on the tangent bundle measures how far parallel transport depends on the path.
On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) the metric fixes one canonical connection, the [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection).
Its curvature is the Riemann curvature, and it vanishes exactly when the metric is locally flat.
links.why: It shows that the Riemann curvature is the curvature of the one connection that the metric determines.

reminder: A rigid monoidal category is a monoidal category in which every object has a left dual and a right dual.
definition: A [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) is rigid if every [object](c:object) $A$ has a left dual and a right dual. A left dual of $A$ is an object $A^*$ with maps $\mathrm{ev}:A^*\otimes A\to I$ and $\mathrm{coev}:I\to A\otimes A^*$ that satisfy the [triangle identities](c:triangle-identities), so $A$ is [dualizable](c:dualizable-object).
examples: The category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field, with $\otimes$, is rigid: the dual of $V$ is $V^*$, with the evaluation and coevaluation maps.
The category of finitely generated projective modules over a commutative ring $R$, with $\otimes_R$, is rigid.
Non-example: The category of all vector spaces is not rigid, because an infinite-dimensional space has no dual object, since the triangle identities would make it finite-dimensional.

steps: Take a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $C$.
Add the condition that every object of $C$ has a left dual and a right dual.
links.why: It shows that rigidity is the one extra condition of duals on every object of a monoidal category.

steps: A [compact closed category](c:compact-closed-category) is a symmetric monoidal category in which every object is dualizable.
The symmetry turns a left dual of each object into a right dual.
So every object has both duals, and the underlying monoidal category is rigid.
links.why: It shows that compact closed categories are the symmetric rigid categories, so they inherit the results on rigid categories.

reminder: A ring homomorphism is a map between rings that preserves sums, products and the unit element.
definition: A ring homomorphism from a [ring](c:ring) $R$ to a ring $S$ is a [function](c:function) $f:R\to S$ with $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$, $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ and $f(1)=1$ for all $a,b\in R$. It follows that $f(0)=0$ and $f(-a)=-f(a)$.
examples: Reduction modulo $n$, $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n$, and the inclusion $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ are ring homomorphisms.
For a commutative ring $R$ and $a\in R$, evaluation $R[x]\to R$, $p\mapsto p(a)$, is a ring homomorphism.
Non-example: The zero map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ preserves sums and products but sends $1$ to $0$, so it is not a ring homomorphism.

steps: A [ring](c:ring) is an algebraic structure with the operations $+$, $\cdot$, $-$, $0$ and $1$.
A [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) of such structures is a map that preserves every operation.
Preserving $+$, $\cdot$ and $1$ is enough, because $f(0)=0$ and $f(-a)=-f(a)$ then follow.
links.why: It shows that a ring homomorphism is the general notion of homomorphism for the signature of rings.

reminder: A ring spectrum is a spectrum with a product and a unit that satisfy the ring laws up to homotopy.
definition: A ring spectrum is a [monoid in a monoidal category](c:monoid-in-a-monoidal-category), namely the [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category) with the [smash product of spectra](c:smash-product-of-spectra). It is a spectrum $E$ with a multiplication $E\wedge E\to E$ and a unit $\mathbb{S}\to E$ from the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum), such that associativity and unit laws hold up to [homotopy](c:homotopy). It is commutative when the multiplication is commutative up to homotopy.
examples: The [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) $\mathbb{S}$ is a ring spectrum, with the canonical isomorphism $\mathbb{S}\wedge\mathbb{S}\cong\mathbb{S}$ as multiplication.
The [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) $HR$ of a ring $R$ is a ring spectrum, with $\pi_0HR=R$.
Complex K-theory $KU$ and complex bordism $MU$ are commutative ring spectra.
Non-example: The suspension $\Sigma\mathbb{S}$ is not a ring spectrum, because its $\pi_0$ is zero, so a unit would be null, and a ring spectrum with null unit is contractible.

steps: Take the [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category) with the smash product of spectra as tensor product.
It is a monoidal category whose unit is the sphere spectrum.
A monoid object in it is a spectrum $E$ with a product $E\wedge E\to E$ and a unit $\mathbb{S}\to E$.
This is the definition of a ring spectrum.
links.why: It shows that a ring spectrum is the general notion of monoid in a monoidal category, in the homotopy category of spectra.

steps: Take an [A-infinity ring](c:a-infinity-ring), a monoid in the stable $(\infty,1)$-category of spectra.
Pass to the homotopy category, which keeps the product and the unit but forgets the higher coherence data.
The product is associative and unital up to homotopy, so the result is a ring spectrum.
links.why: It shows that every A-infinity ring has an underlying ring spectrum, so results on ring spectra apply to it.

reminder: A root of a polynomial is a value of the variable at which the polynomial equals zero.
definition: A root of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ with coefficients in a [field](c:field) $K$, or in a ring, is an element $r$ with $p(r)=0$. An $n$-th root of $a$ is a root of the polynomial $x^n-a$.
examples: The numbers $2$ and $3$ are roots of $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$.
The number $i$ is a root of $x^2+1$ over $\mathbb{C}$.
Non-example: The number $\sqrt2$ is not a root of $x^2-2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, because $\sqrt2$ is not in $\mathbb{Q}$, although it is a root over $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Take an element $a$ of a ring $R$ and the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p(x)=x^2-a$.
An element $r$ is a root of $p$ exactly when $r^2-a=0$.
That says $r^2=a$, so $r$ is a [square root](c:square-root) of $a$.
links.why: It shows that square roots are the roots of the polynomials $x^2-a$, so facts on roots apply to them.

steps: Take the polynomial $x^n-1$ over a ring $R$.
A root of it is an element $r$ with $r^n=1$.
That is an $n$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity).
links.why: It shows that roots of unity are the roots of the polynomials $x^n-1$.

reminder: A rooted tree is a tree in which one vertex is marked as the root.
definition: A rooted tree is a [tree](c:tree), a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) with no cycles, together with one chosen [vertex](c:vertex) called the root. Every other vertex has a unique parent, the next vertex on the path to the root.
examples: A family tree drawn from one ancestor is a rooted tree: the ancestor is the root, and the parent of a person is the next vertex towards it.
A binary search tree is a rooted tree in which the top key is the root and every key has at most two children.
Non-example: A cycle with one marked vertex is not a rooted tree, because the cycle is not a tree.

steps: Take a [tree](c:tree) $T$.
Choose any vertex $r$ of $T$ and call it the root.
Orient each edge towards $r$ to get the parent relation; the added data is the choice of $r$.
links.why: It shows that a rooted tree is a tree with one extra choice, which gives the tree a direction and a parent relation.

reminder: The Schrödinger equation gives the change in time of a wave function $\psi$ by $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi=H\psi$ for the energy operator $H$.
definition: For a particle of mass $m$ in a potential $V$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the wave function $\psi(x,t)$ obeys the [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation) $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta\psi+V\psi$. It comes from the energy $E=\frac{p^2}{2m}+V$ when $E$ is replaced by $i\hbar\,\partial_t$ and $p$ by $-i\hbar\nabla$. In general it reads $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi=H\psi$, where $H$ is a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) that is a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
examples: A free particle, with $V=0$, has plane-wave solutions $\psi=e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ with $\hbar\omega=\hbar^2k^2/2m$.
The harmonic oscillator $V=\frac12m\omega^2x^2$ has stationary solutions $e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\phi_n(x)$ with $E_n=\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)$.
Non-example: The heat equation $\partial_tu=\Delta u$ has no factor $i$, and its solutions smooth out and lose $L^2$ norm, while solutions of the Schrödinger equation keep it.

steps: Divide by $i\hbar$ to write the equation as $\partial_t\psi=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H\psi$.
This has the form $\partial_tf=Lf$ of an [evolution equation](c:evolution-equation) with $L=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H$.
Because $H$ is self-adjoint, $L$ is skew-adjoint, so the solution operators are unitary and keep the norm of $\psi$ constant.
links.why: It shows that the Schrödinger equation is the evolution equation with generator $-iH/\hbar$, which explains the conservation of probability.

reminder: A section of a morphism $f:A\to B$ is a morphism $\sigma:B\to A$ with $f\circ\sigma=\mathrm{id}_B$.
definition: Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in a [category](c:category). A section of $f$ is a morphism $\sigma:B\to A$ such that the [composition](c:composition) $f\circ\sigma$ is the [identity morphism](c:identity-morphism) of $B$. So $\sigma$ is a right inverse of $f$.
examples: For a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $p:E\to M$, a section is a map $s:M\to E$ with $p\circ s=\mathrm{id}_M$, which chooses one vector in each fibre.
The projection $A\times B\to A$ has the section $a\mapsto(a,b_0)$ for any fixed $b_0\in B$.
Non-example: The reduction $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2$ has no section among abelian groups, because a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}$ is zero, although it has a section as a map of sets.

steps: Take a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $p:E\to M$ in the category of manifolds with $n$ times continuously differentiable maps.
A $C^n$ section is a $C^n$ map $s:M\to E$ with $p\circ s=\mathrm{id}_M$.
That is a section of the morphism $p$ in this category.
links.why: It shows that sections of bundles are the categorical sections of the bundle projection.

reminder: The Selberg sieve bounds above the number of integers with no small prime factor, using squares of weighted divisor sums.
definition: Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite set of integers, $P$ a product of [primes](c:prime-number), and $y$ the level. Choose real weights $\lambda_d$ on the [squarefree](c:squarefree-integer) divisors $d$ of $P$ with $\lambda_1=1$ and $\lambda_d=0$ for $d>\sqrt y$; then the number of $n\in\mathcal A$ coprime to $P$ is at most $\sum_{n\in\mathcal A}\big(\sum_{d\mid\gcd(n,P)}\lambda_d\big)^2$. The Selberg sieve chooses the weights that minimize this [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form), and the level $y$ controls the size of the error term.
examples: The number of $n\le x$ for which $n$ and $n+2$ are both prime is $O(x/(\log x)^2)$, and the Selberg sieve proves this upper bound.
The Brun-Titchmarsh bound says that the number of primes $p\le x$ with $p\equiv a\pmod q$ is at most about $2x/(\varphi(q)\log(x/q))$, and the Selberg sieve gives it.
Non-example: The Selberg upper bound sieve cannot prove that twin primes exist, because it gives only an upper bound for the sifted set and never a positive lower bound.

reminder: A semialgebraic set is a finite Boolean combination of sets defined by polynomial equations and inequalities.
definition: Let $R$ be an [ordered field](c:ordered-field). A subset of $R^n$ is semialgebraic if it is a finite union of sets $\{x:p(x)=0,\ q_1(x)>0,\dots,q_k(x)>0\}$ with $p,q_i$ [polynomials](c:polynomial) over $R$. Equivalently, the semialgebraic sets form the smallest [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) of subsets of $R^n$ that contains all sets $\{p>0\}$.
examples: The closed unit disc $\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is semialgebraic: it is given by one polynomial inequality.
The graph $\{(x,\sqrt x):x\ge0\}$ is semialgebraic, because it equals $\{y^2=x,\ y\ge0\}$.

Non-example: The graph $\{(x,\sin x)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not semialgebraic, because it meets the line $y=0$ in the infinite discrete set $\pi\mathbb{Z}$, but a semialgebraic subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is a finite union of points and intervals.

steps: Take polynomials $p_1,\dots,p_k$ over $R$ and their common [zero locus](c:zero-locus) $Z=\{x:p_1(x)=\dots=p_k(x)=0\}$.
Each set $\{p_i=0\}$ is a basic semialgebraic set.
The set $Z$ is the finite intersection of these sets, and intersections are allowed, so $Z$ is semialgebraic.
links.why: It shows that every zero set of polynomials in $R^n$ is semialgebraic, and that the inequalities add genuinely new sets such as discs.

reminder: A seminorm is a nonnegative function on a vector space that is homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality.
definition: A seminorm on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is a function $p:V\to[0,\infty)$ with $p(av)=|a|\,p(v)$ and $p(u+v)\le p(u)+p(v)$ for all scalars $a$ and all vectors $u,v$. It is a [norm](c:norm) except that $p(v)=0$ may hold for a vector $v\ne0$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the function $p(x,y)=|x|$ is a seminorm, and it vanishes on the whole $y$-axis.
For each point $a\in[0,1]$, the function $f\mapsto|f(a)|$ is a seminorm on the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$.
The function $f\mapsto\int_0^1|f|\,dx$ on Riemann-integrable functions is a seminorm, and it vanishes on functions that are zero except at finitely many points.
Non-example: The function $p(x)=\sqrt{|x|}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ satisfies the triangle inequality but is not homogeneous, because $p(4x)=2p(x)\ne4p(x)$.

steps: Take a [norm](c:norm) $\|\cdot\|$ on a vector space $V$.
It is nonnegative, homogeneous and subadditive, which are the three conditions of a seminorm.
So every norm is a seminorm, and a norm adds the condition that only $0$ has size $0$.
links.why: It shows that seminorms are norms without definiteness, so they also measure sizes modulo a subspace.

steps: Let $p$ be a seminorm and let $s,t\ge0$ with $s+t=1$.
Then $p(su+tv)\le p(su)+p(tv)=s\,p(u)+t\,p(v)$ by subadditivity and homogeneity.
This is the defining inequality of a [convex function](c:convex-function), so every seminorm is convex.
links.why: It shows that every seminorm is a convex function, so its unit ball is a convex set.

reminder: A semisimple algebra is an algebra over a field whose Jacobson radical is zero.
definition: An [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ with unit over a [field](c:field) $k$ is semisimple if its [Jacobson radical](c:jacobson-radical), the intersection of its maximal left ideals, is zero. For finite-dimensional $A$, this holds exactly when $A$ is a finite product of matrix algebras over [division algebras](c:division-algebra).
examples: The matrix algebra $M_n(k)$ over a field $k$ is semisimple.
The [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $\mathbb{C}[G]$ of a finite group $G$ is semisimple, and it is isomorphic to a product of matrix algebras $M_{n_i}(\mathbb{C})$.
Non-example: The algebra $k[x]/(x^2)$ is not semisimple, because its Jacobson radical is the ideal $(x)\ne0$.

steps: Let $A$ be a [simple algebra](c:simple-algebra) over a field, so its only two-sided ideals are $0$ and $A$.
The [Jacobson radical](c:jacobson-radical) of $A$ is a two-sided ideal, so it is $0$ or $A$.
It is not $A$, because an algebra with unit has a maximal left ideal, so the radical is $0$ and $A$ is semisimple.
links.why: It shows that every simple algebra is semisimple, and that semisimple algebras are the products of simple ones in the finite-dimensional case.

reminder: A separable Banach space is a Banach space that has a countable subset whose closure is the whole space.
definition: A [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ is separable if it contains a countable [dense](c:dense-set) subset $D$, so that every point of $X$ is a limit of a sequence in $D$. Equivalently, $X$ is separable as a topological space for the norm topology.
examples: The sequence spaces $\ell^p$ with $1\le p<\infty$ are separable, because the finitely supported sequences with rational terms are dense.
The space $C[0,1]$ is separable, because polynomials with rational coefficients are dense by the Weierstrass theorem.
Non-example: The space $\ell^\infty$ is not separable, because the uncountably many sequences of $0$ and $1$ are at distance $1$ from each other, so no countable set is dense.

steps: Take a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$.
Add the condition that $X$ has a countable dense subset.
links.why: It shows that separability is the one condition that lets a countable set of vectors approximate every vector.

steps: A Banach space is a metric space, so it is a topological space for the norm topology.
A topological space is separable when it has a countable dense subset, which is the defining condition of a separable Banach space.
So a separable Banach space is a Banach space that is separable as a topological space.
links.why: It shows that general facts on separable spaces, such as the countability of a dense set, apply to separable Banach spaces.

reminder: A separable metric space is a metric space that has a countable dense subset.
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) is separable if it has a countable [dense](c:dense-set) subset. Equivalently, a topological space is a separable metric space when it is both [separable](c:separable-space) and [metrizable](c:metrizable-space), and for metric spaces this is the same as being [second-countable](c:second-countable-space).
examples: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a separable metric space, with $\mathbb{Q}^n$ as a countable dense subset.
Every subspace of a separable metric space is a separable metric space.
Non-example: An uncountable set with the discrete metric $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$ is not separable, because its only dense subset is the whole set.

steps: Take a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$.
Add the condition that $X$ has a countable dense subset.
links.why: It shows that separability is the one extra condition on a metric space, and that it gives a countable base.

steps: Let $X$ be a [Polish space](c:polish-space), that is a separable space with a compatible complete metric $d$.
Keep the metric $d$ and forget that it is complete.
Then $(X,d)$ is a metric space with a countable dense subset, so it is a separable metric space.
links.why: It shows that Polish spaces are the separable metric spaces whose metric can be chosen complete.

steps: Let $X$ be a [separable Banach space](c:separable-banach-space) with norm $\|\cdot\|$.
The formula $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ defines a metric whose topology is the norm topology.
A countable dense subset of $X$ stays dense for $d$, so $(X,d)$ is a separable metric space.
links.why: It shows that every separable Banach space is a separable metric space, so facts on separable metric spaces apply to it.

reminder: A set partition splits a set into nonempty blocks that do not overlap and together cover the set.
definition: A partition of a [set](c:set) $S$ is a collection of nonempty [subsets](c:subset), called blocks, such that any two different blocks are disjoint and the [union](c:union) of all blocks is $S$. Equivalently, every element of $S$ lies in exactly one block.
examples: The family $\{\{1,3\},\{2\},\{4,5\}\}$ is a partition of $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ with three blocks.
The equivalence classes of an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) on a set form a partition of the set, and a set with 3 elements has exactly 5 partitions.
Non-example: The family $\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ is not a partition of $\{1,2,3\}$, because the two blocks overlap in $2$.

reminder: A short map between metric spaces never increases distances.
definition: A short map from a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d_X)$ to a metric space $(Y,d_Y)$ is a [function](c:function) $f:X\to Y$ with $d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le d_X(x,x')$ for all $x,x'\in X$. It is also called a non-expanding map or a 1-Lipschitz map.
examples: The identity map of a metric space, and the inclusion of a subspace, are short maps.
The projection $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, $(x,y)\mapsto x$, is short for the Euclidean metrics.
For a fixed point $x_0$ of a metric space $X$, the map $x\mapsto d(x,x_0)$ from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is short, by the triangle inequality.
Non-example: The map $x\mapsto2x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not short, because it doubles the distance between $0$ and $1$.

steps: A [Lipschitz function](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) satisfies $d(f(x),f(y))\le K\,d(x,y)$ for some constant $K$.
Choose the constant $K=1$.
The result is a short map, so the added condition is that the Lipschitz constant is at most $1$.
links.why: It shows that short maps are the Lipschitz maps with constant 1, which form the morphisms of a category of metric spaces.

steps: Let $f$ be an [isometry](c:isometry), so $d(f(x),f(y))=d(x,y)$ for all $x,y$.
Then in particular $d(f(x),f(y))\le d(x,y)$.
So $f$ is a short map, and isometries are the short maps that keep every distance exactly.
links.why: It shows that isometries are short maps, so facts proved for short maps cover isometries.

reminder: A sigma-discrete base is a base of a topology that is a countable union of discrete families of open sets.
definition: A family $\mathcal D$ of subsets of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is discrete if every point of $X$ has a neighbourhood that meets at most one member of $\mathcal D$. A $\sigma$-discrete [base](c:base) is a base $\mathcal B$ of the topology of $X$ with $\mathcal B=\bigcup_n\mathcal B_n$, where each $\mathcal B_n$ is a discrete family of [open sets](c:open-set).
examples: Every countable base is $\sigma$-discrete, because we can put one set in each $\mathcal B_n$, and a family with one member is discrete.
Every [metric space](c:metric-space) has a $\sigma$-discrete base, and Bing's theorem says that this characterizes the metrizable spaces among the regular spaces.

Non-example: The family of all open intervals of $\mathbb{R}$ is a base but not $\sigma$-discrete, because a discrete family of nonempty open sets in $\mathbb{R}$ is countable, and this family is not.

steps: Take a [base](c:base) $\mathcal B$ of the topology of $X$.
Require that $\mathcal B$ splits into countably many subfamilies.
Require that each subfamily is discrete: every point has a neighbourhood that meets at most one member.
links.why: It shows that a sigma-discrete base is a base with a countable decomposition into locally small pieces.

reminder: A measure is sigma-finite when the whole space is a countable union of sets of finite measure.
definition: A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$ is $\sigma$-finite if there are measurable sets $A_1,A_2,\dots$ with $\mu(A_i)<\infty$ for every $i$ and $\bigcup_iA_i=X$.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is $\sigma$-finite: take $A_i=[-i,i]$.
Every [finite measure](c:finite-measure), such as a probability measure, is $\sigma$-finite.
Non-example: Counting measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is not $\sigma$-finite, because sets of finite measure are finite, and countably many finite sets cannot cover the uncountable set $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Let $\mu$ be a [finite measure](c:finite-measure) on $X$, so $\mu(X)<\infty$.
Put $A_i=X$ for every $i$.
Then $\mu(A_i)<\infty$ and $\bigcup_iA_i=X$, so $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite.
links.why: It shows that every finite measure is sigma-finite, so theorems proved for sigma-finite measures cover probability measures.

steps: Take a [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on a measurable space $X$.
Add the condition that $X$ is a countable union of sets of finite measure.
links.why: It shows that sigma-finiteness is the one condition that lets us work piece by piece with finite measures.

reminder: The number of sign changes of a real sequence is the number of times neighbouring nonzero terms differ in sign.
definition: For a finite [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_0,\dots,a_n)$ of [real numbers](c:real-number), delete all terms that are zero. The number of sign changes is the number of neighbouring pairs in the remaining sequence whose members have opposite signs, one positive and one negative.
examples: The sequence $(1,-2,3,0,-4)$ becomes $(1,-2,3,-4)$ when the zero is deleted, so it has $3$ sign changes.
In Sturm's theorem, the number of sign changes of the Sturm chain at $x$ is called $V(x)$, and $V(a)-V(b)$ counts the distinct real roots of the polynomial in $(a,b]$.
Non-example: The number of negative terms is not the number of sign changes, because $(-1,-2,-3)$ has three negative terms and no sign change.

reminder: A simple algebra is a nonzero algebra whose only two-sided ideals are zero and the whole algebra.
definition: A unital [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $k$ is simple if it is a simple object in the category of $A$-$A$-[bimodules](c:bimodule). That is, $A\ne0$ and the only two-sided [ideals](c:ideal) of $A$ are $0$ and $A$.
examples: The matrix algebra $M_n(k)$ over a field $k$ is simple.
Every [division algebra](c:division-algebra), such as the quaternions over $\mathbb{R}$, is simple.
Non-example: The algebra $k\times k$ is not simple, because $k\times0$ is a two-sided ideal that is neither $0$ nor the whole algebra.

steps: Let $A$ be a simple algebra over a field $k$.
The [Jacobson radical](c:jacobson-radical) of $A$ is a two-sided ideal, so it is $0$ or $A$.
It is not $A$, because an algebra with unit has a maximal left ideal, so the radical is $0$ and $A$ is semisimple.
links.why: It shows that every simple algebra is semisimple, so results on semisimple algebras apply to it.

steps: Let $D$ be a [division algebra](c:division-algebra), so every nonzero element of $D$ has an inverse.
A two-sided ideal that contains a nonzero element contains its inverse, so it contains $1$ and equals $D$.
So the only two-sided ideals of $D$ are $0$ and $D$, and $D$ is simple.
links.why: It shows that division algebras are the simplest simple algebras, so they are the first examples to test a claim.

reminder: A simplicial abelian group is a sequence of abelian groups with face and degeneracy homomorphisms that satisfy the simplicial identities.
definition: A simplicial abelian group is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in the category of abelian groups, that is a functor $A:\Delta^{op}\to\mathrm{Ab}$. It consists of [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) $A_n$ for $n\ge0$ with face maps $d_i:A_n\to A_{n-1}$ and degeneracy maps $s_i:A_n\to A_{n+1}$ that are [group homomorphisms](c:group-homomorphism) and satisfy the simplicial identities.
examples: For a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) $X$, the free simplicial abelian group $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ has as $n$-th group the free abelian group on $X_n$.
For an abelian group $A$, the constant simplicial abelian group has $A_n=A$ for all $n$ and all face and degeneracy maps equal to the identity.
Non-example: The standard 1-simplex $\Delta^1$ is a simplicial set, not a simplicial abelian group, because $s_0$ would be an injective homomorphism from a group of order 2 into a group of order 3.

steps: A [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in a category $C$ is a functor $\Delta^{op}\to C$.
Take $C$ to be the category of abelian groups.
Then each level is an abelian group, and each face and degeneracy map is a group homomorphism.
links.why: It shows that a simplicial abelian group is a simplicial object in the category of abelian groups, so levelwise algebra applies.

steps: A [simplicial group](c:simplicial-group) is a simplicial object in the category of groups.
An abelian group is a group, and a homomorphism of abelian groups is a group homomorphism.
So a simplicial abelian group is a simplicial group whose levels are all abelian.
links.why: It shows that simplicial abelian groups are the abelian case of simplicial groups, so their homotopy theory is the simplest one.

reminder: The sinc function is $\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$, with value $1$ at $x=0$.
definition: The normalized sinc function is $\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ for $x\ne0$ and $\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$, where $\sin$ is the [sine](c:sine) function. It is continuous, it is zero exactly at the nonzero integers, and its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) is the indicator function of $[-\frac12,\frac12]$ for the convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx$. Some authors use the unnormalized function $\sin(x)/x$.
examples: The value $\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$ is the limit of $\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ as $x\to0$, so the function is continuous at $0$.
In the sampling theorem, a band-limited signal is rebuilt as $f(t)=\sum_nf(nT)\operatorname{sinc}((t-nT)/T)$ when the sample spacing $T$ is small enough.
Non-example: The function $\sin(\pi x)/x$ is not the normalized sinc function, because it takes the value $\pi$ at $0$.

reminder: A sliding block code replaces each symbol of a bi-infinite sequence by a function of a fixed finite window around it.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite alphabets and $X\subseteq A^{\mathbb Z}$ a [shift space](c:shift-space). A sliding block code is a map $\phi:X\to B^{\mathbb Z}$ with $\phi(x)_i=\Phi(x_{i-m},\dots,x_{i+n})$ for all $i$, where $\Phi:A^{m+n+1}\to B$ is a fixed block map. So each output symbol depends on the same finite window of the input, and $\phi$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) for the [product topology](c:product-topology) and commutes with the shift.
examples: The map $\phi(x)_i=x_i+x_{i+1}\pmod 2$ on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ is a sliding block code with a window of two symbols.
The shift $\sigma(x)_i=x_{i+1}$ and the identity map are sliding block codes.
Non-example: The map with $\phi(x)_i=1$ if and only if $x_j=1$ for some $j\ge i$ is not a sliding block code, because no finite window decides the output symbol, and the map is not continuous.

steps: Fix a coordinate $i$; the output symbol $\phi(x)_i$ depends only on the symbols $x_{i-m},\dots,x_{i+n}$.
So the preimage of a cylinder set is a union of cylinder sets of $X$, which are open in the [product topology](c:product-topology).
Cylinder sets form a base, so the preimage of every open set is open and $\phi$ is continuous.
links.why: It shows that every sliding block code is continuous, which is one half of the Curtis-Hedlund-Lyndon characterization.

steps: Let $\sigma$ be the shift, which acts on both $X$ and $B^{\mathbb Z}$ and generates an action of the group $\mathbb Z$.
Then we get $\phi(\sigma x)_i=\Phi(x_{i+1-m},\dots,x_{i+1+n})=\phi(x)_{i+1}=\sigma(\phi(x))_i$ for every $i$.
So $\phi\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ\phi$, and $\phi$ is an [equivariant map](c:equivariant-map) for the shift action.
links.why: It shows that every sliding block code commutes with the shift, which is the other half of the Curtis-Hedlund-Lyndon characterization.

reminder: The slope of a coherent sheaf on a curve is its degree divided by its rank.
definition: For a [coherent sheaf](c:coherent-sheaf) $E$ of positive rank on a smooth projective [curve](c:curve), the slope is the rational number $\mu(E)=\deg(E)/\operatorname{rk}(E)$. Here $\deg(E)$ is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-coherent-sheaf) and $\operatorname{rk}(E)$ is the [rank](c:rank-of-a-coherent-sheaf) of $E$.
examples: On the projective line, the line bundle $\mathcal O(d)$ has degree $d$ and rank $1$, so its slope is $d$.
The sheaf $\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(1)$ has degree $1$ and rank $2$, so its slope is $\frac12$.
Non-example: A skyscraper sheaf at a point has rank $0$ and degree $1$, so $\deg/\operatorname{rk}$ is not defined, although some authors set the slope to $\infty$.

reminder: An object is small when it is $\kappa$-compact for some regular cardinal $\kappa$, so maps out of it commute with $\kappa$-filtered colimits.
definition: Let $\kappa$ be a [regular cardinal](c:is-regular). An object $X$ of a [category](c:category) is $\kappa$-compact if the [hom-functor](c:hom-functor) $\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)$ preserves $\kappa$-filtered [colimits](c:colimit). The object $X$ is small if it is $\kappa$-compact for some regular cardinal $\kappa$, and then also for every larger regular cardinal.
examples: In the category of sets every set $X$ is small: it is $\kappa$-compact for every regular cardinal $\kappa>|X|$.
In the category of groups, and in the category of modules over a ring, every object is small.

Non-example: In the opposite category $\mathrm{Set}^{op}$ the two-point set $2$ is not small, because for each regular cardinal $\kappa$ the chain of the sets $\kappa\setminus\alpha$ for $\alpha<\kappa$ has colimit $\emptyset$ there, but $\operatorname{colim}_\alpha\mathrm{Hom}(2,Y_\alpha)$ has at least two elements.

steps: Let $X$ be a [compact object](c:compact-object), so $\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)$ preserves [filtered colimits](c:filtered-colimit).
Filtered colimits are the $\aleph_0$-filtered colimits, and $\aleph_0$ is a regular cardinal.
So $X$ is $\aleph_0$-compact, and therefore small.
links.why: It shows that compact objects are the small objects that work for the smallest cardinal, so they satisfy the hypotheses of the small object argument.

reminder: The Smith normal form of a matrix over a principal ideal domain is an equivalent diagonal matrix with each entry dividing the next.
definition: Let $R$ be a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) and $A$ a [matrix](c:matrix) over $R$ of size $n\times m$. The Smith normal form of $A$ is the [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) $D=PAQ$ with nonzero entries $d_1,\dots,d_r$ followed by zeros, where each $d_i$ [divides](c:divisibility) $d_{i+1}$ and $P$ and $Q$ are invertible matrices over $R$. It exists for every $A$, and the $d_i$ are unique up to units.
examples: Over $\mathbb{Z}$, the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\6&8\end{pmatrix}$ has the Smith normal form $\operatorname{diag}(2,4)$.
A diagonal matrix such as $\operatorname{diag}(1,3,6)$, in which each entry divides the next, is its own Smith normal form.
Over a field, the Smith normal form of a matrix $A$ is a diagonal matrix with $\operatorname{rank}A$ entries $1$ followed by zeros.
Non-example: The matrix $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is diagonal but not in Smith normal form, because $2$ does not divide $3$; its Smith normal form is $\operatorname{diag}(1,6)$.

reminder: A smooth algebra over a field is a finitely presented algebra that is formally smooth: maps out of it lift along square-zero extensions.
definition: A commutative algebra $A$ over a [field](c:field) $k$ is smooth if it is finitely presented and [formally smooth](c:formally-smooth): every $k$-algebra map $A\to B/I$ with $I^2=0$ lifts to a $k$-algebra map $A\to B$. Equivalently, the morphism $\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a [smooth morphism of schemes](c:smooth).
examples: The polynomial algebra $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field $k$ is smooth.
The coordinate ring $k[x,y]/(x^2+y^2-1)$ of the circle is smooth when the characteristic of $k$ is not $2$.
Non-example: The algebra $k[x,y]/(xy)$ is not smooth, because the origin is a singular point, where all partial derivatives of $xy$ vanish.

steps: Take a $k$-algebra $A$ and the morphism of schemes $\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$.
This morphism is [smooth](c:smooth) exactly when $A$ is finitely presented and formally smooth over $k$.
So a smooth algebra is the case of a smooth morphism with an affine source and the spectrum of a field as base.
links.why: It shows that smooth algebras are the affine pieces of smooth varieties over a field.

reminder: A smooth partition of unity is a family of smooth nonnegative functions with locally finite supports that sum to one.
definition: A smooth partition of unity on a set $s$ in a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a family $(f_i)$ of [smooth functions](c:smooth-function) $M\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f_i\ge0$ whose [supports](c:support) form a [locally finite family](c:locally-finite-family). It satisfies $\sum_if_i(x)=1$ for every $x\in s$ and $\sum_if_i(x)\le1$ for every $x\in M$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, let $\psi$ be a smooth function with $0\le\psi\le1$ that is $0$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $1$ on $[1,\infty)$; then $\psi$ and $1-\psi$ form a smooth partition of unity.
On the circle, two smooth bump functions that are positive on two arcs covering the circle give a smooth partition of unity after division by their sum.
Non-example: The constant functions $f_n=2^{-n}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are smooth and nonnegative and sum to $1$, but their supports are all of $\mathbb{R}$, so they are not locally finite.

steps: A [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) is a family of continuous nonnegative functions with locally finite supports and sum $1$.
Take the space to be a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold).
Require that every function is smooth instead of only continuous.
links.why: It shows that smooth partitions of unity are the partitions of unity with smooth functions, so they let us glue smooth local data.

reminder: A social choice function maps each profile of voters' preference orders to one winning alternative.
definition: Let $A$ be a finite set of alternatives and $N$ a set of voters. A profile gives each voter a [preference relation](c:preference-relation) on $A$ that is a [total order](c:total-order). A social choice function is a [function](c:function) from profiles to $A$, or to nonempty subsets of $A$, that returns the winning alternative or alternatives of each profile.
examples: Plurality rule returns the alternative with most first places, with ties broken by a fixed order of the alternatives.
A dictatorship of voter $1$ returns the top alternative of voter $1$ for every profile.
Non-example: A map that returns a ranking of all alternatives is a [social welfare function](c:social-welfare-function), not a social choice function.

reminder: A social welfare function maps each profile of voters' preference orders to one social preference order.
definition: Let $A$ be a set of alternatives and $N$ a set of voters. A social welfare function is a [function](c:function) that sends each profile of individual [preference relations](c:preference-relation), one [total order](c:total-order) on $A$ for each voter, to a single social total order on $A$.
examples: A dictatorship of voter $1$ is a social welfare function: the social order is the order of voter $1$.
Majority rule on two alternatives, with an odd number of voters, ranks $a$ above $b$ when more voters prefer $a$.
Non-example: Pairwise majority voting on three alternatives is not a social welfare function, because the profiles $a>b>c$, $b>c>a$ and $c>a>b$ give a cycle, which is not an order.

reminder: A solid of revolution is the solid swept out when a plane region turns once around an axis in its plane.
definition: Let $R$ be a region of a [plane](c:plane) and $L$ a [line](c:line) in that plane that does not cross the interior of $R$. The solid of revolution is the set of points that $R$ sweeps out in a full [rotation](c:rotation) of angle $2\pi$ about the axis $L$.
examples: A rectangle turned about one of its sides gives a cylinder.
A right triangle turned about one of its legs gives a cone.
A disc that does not meet the axis, turned about the axis, gives a torus.
Non-example: A cube is not a solid of revolution, because it is not invariant under all rotations about any axis.

reminder: A functor satisfies the solution set condition when, for each object $d$, some set of maps $d\to G(c_i)$ factors every map $d\to G(c)$.
definition: Let $G:C\to D$ be a [functor](c:functor) with $C$ locally small. It satisfies the solution set condition if for each object $d$ of $D$ there is a set of objects $c_i$ of $C$ and maps $f_i:d\to G(c_i)$ such that every map $f:d\to G(c)$ equals $G(h)\circ f_i$ for some $i$ and some map $h:c_i\to c$. By Freyd's theorem, when $C$ is a [complete category](c:complete-category) and $G$ preserves limits, this condition holds exactly when $G$ has a left [adjoint functor](c:adjoint-functor).
examples: The forgetful functor from groups to sets satisfies it: for a set $X$, the groups generated by the image of a map from $X$ have at most $\max(|X|,\aleph_0)$ elements, so up to isomorphism there is only a set of them.
Every functor that has a left adjoint satisfies it, with the single unit map $d\to G(F(d))$.

Non-example: The forgetful functor from complete lattices to sets does not satisfy it, because it preserves limits but has no left adjoint, since the free complete lattice on three generators does not exist.

steps: Let $G$ have a left [adjoint functor](c:adjoint-functor) $F$, with unit maps $\eta_d:d\to G(F(d))$.
Take the one-element set $\{\eta_d\}$ for each object $d$.
Every map $f:d\to G(c)$ equals $G(\bar f)\circ\eta_d$, where $\bar f:F(d)\to c$ is the adjunct of $f$.
So a right adjoint satisfies the solution set condition, and Freyd's theorem is a partial converse.
links.why: It shows that the solution set condition is a weakening of having a left adjoint that is easy to check on generators.
